//: The full-tank economy rule exists twice: FuelEconomy in Dart, which is what
the app shows, and economy.ts in the dispatch-webhooks edge function, which
is what a webhook says about the same fill-up. One is Flutter and the other
is Deno, so neither can import the other, and a figure in a chat window that
disagrees with the one on the phone is a bug nobody would find from either
side. Both suites read this file instead:
test/domain/fuel/economy_fixture_test.dart
supabase/functions/dispatch-webhooks/economy_test.ts
Every expected value was worked out by hand, with the working beside it.
Never paste in what an implementation printed: a fixture generated by the
code it checks can only ever agree with it. The one exception is marked as
such where it appears: `readings.halves`, where the question is what the
app's own arithmetic does and the app is therefore the answer.
Rows are shaped like fuel_entries rows, in canonical units. `volume_l` is
kilowatt-hours for an electric car. `primary_fuel_key` is what the app hands
FuelEconomy.compute: the vehicle's main fuel when it takes two, else null.
`expected` is the point anchored at `closing_id`, or null when there is none.

spans.name: a full tank to the next full tank
an ordinary tank, to the last decimal
spans.working: 49680 - 48978 = 702 km. 42.8 / 702 = 107 / 1755; long division of 10700 by 1755 gives 6, then the digits 096866 repeating, so 6.096866096866...

spans.name: partial fills in between add their volume
spans.working: 15 + 10.5 + 20 = 45.5 l over 500 km is 9.1. The opening tank's 40 l was burned before the span began.

spans.name: a missed fill inside the span means no figure
spans.working: Fuel went in unlogged before c2, so 42 l over 500 km would flatter the car.

spans.name: a missed fill on the closing entry means no figure
spans.working: The flag sits on the entry that closes the span, which is inside it.

spans.name: a missed fill on the opening tank does not reach the span it opens
spans.working: d2's flag spoils the span d1 to d2, which ends there. d2 to d3 is 30 l over 500 km, 6.0.

spans.name: a closing entry that is not a full tank has no figure
spans.working: Nobody knows how much room was left in the tank after e2.

spans.name: the first full tank has nothing to measure from
spans.working: A partial fill cannot open a span, so g2 is the baseline and not a result.

spans.name: no distance since the previous full tank is no figure, however far back the one before
spans.working: The span that closes at x2 opened at x1, 0 km earlier. It does not reach back to x0 for a distance it can divide by.

spans.name: two fuels interleaved: the petrol span ignores the LPG between
spans.working: Petrol chain p1 to p2: 25 l over 500 km is 5.0. Blended with l1 it would be 75 l, 15.0.

spans.name: two fuels interleaved: and the LPG span ignores the petrol
spans.working: LPG chain l1 to l2: 45 l over 1700 - 1200 = 500 km is 9.0.

spans.name: a partial fill counts towards its own fuel only
spans.working: Petrol: 10 + 20 = 30 l over 500 km is 6.0. The 12 l of LPG at 1300 km is the other chain's.

spans.name: an unnamed fill is the main fuel on a car that takes two
spans.working: n1 was logged before the second tank existed and carries no fuel; with petrol as the main fuel it opens the petrol chain. 25 l over 500 km is 5.0.

spans.name: and a chain of its own when no main fuel is given
spans.working: With no main fuel the unnamed q1 and the petrol q2 are different chains, so q2 is the first full tank of its own and has no baseline.

spans.name: entries in any order, with a later fill already logged
spans.working: By odometer: h1 1000, h2 1500, h3 2000, h4 2500. The span closing at h3 is 35 + 30 = 65 l over 1000 km, 6.5; h4 comes after it and is not its business.

spans.name: at the same odometer and day a full tank sorts before a partial
spans.working: Order is i1, i2, i3: the 5 l partial lands after the full tank it shares a reading with, so the span closing at i2 is 30 l over 500 km, 6.0. Sorted the other way it would be 35 l, 7.0.

spans.name: at the same odometer an earlier day sorts first, a partial fill included
spans.working: The date is compared before the full-tank tie-break. Order is j1, j2 (8 January), j3 (10 January): the partial was two days before the full tank it shares a reading with, so it is inside the span closing at j3. 10 + 20 = 30 l over 500 km, 6.0. Ordered by full-before-partial alone it would fall outside: 20 l, 4.0.

spans.name: an electric car is the same arithmetic in kilowatt-hours
spans.working: 54 kWh over 12300 - 12000 = 300 km is 54 / 300 * 100 = 18.0 kWh per 100 km. Nothing is inverted or converted.

//: How one figure reads in each household's units. The app converts in
lib/core/format/unit_format.dart and the webhook message in chat_message.ts,
from constants each of them had to write down for itself.

cases.name: kilometres and litres read per 100 km
miles and US gallons invert to mpg
miles and UK gallons use the larger gallon
kilometres with gallons is still mpg
miles with litres has no gallon of its own and gets the US one
and per 100 miles, never inverted to mpg

halves//: What the APP prints when the digit to drop is a 5. Not worked by hand: these
are the app's own output, recorded, because at a half the two platforms'
formatters part ways and the app is the one a household has in its hand.
`intl` takes the fraction off the number, multiplies it up and rounds that,
all in binary floating point. JavaScript's Intl rounds the shortest decimal
spelling instead, so it turns 6.35 into 6.4 where the app says 6.3, and
`toFixed` rounds the exact binary value, so it turns 1.95 into 1.9 where the
app says 2.0. Over two million values neither agreed with the app
everywhere; repeating intl's own three steps did. If an `intl` upgrade ever
changes these, the Dart test fails first, and both sides move together.

halves.name: a half that binary holds exactly rounds away from zero
6.35 is stored a hair under the half, and what is stored is what gets rounded
1.95, a moped, lands on the half once the fraction is multiplied up
